meta.title: Who really said "Water, water everywhere and not a drop to drink"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Coleridge's real line is "Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink." The popular "and not a drop to drink" is a smoothed-out misquote.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Water, water everywhere and not a drop to drink'?
meta.ogDescription: The idea is Coleridge's, from 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798) — but he wrote 'Nor any drop to drink,' not 'and not a drop to drink.'

answer.label: Not quite Coleridge — a misquote of the real line
answer.sourceLine: The image is genuinely Coleridge’s — it comes from “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” (1798) — but he did not write it this way. The real lines read “Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.” The familiar “everywhere and not a drop to drink” is a smoothed-out paraphrase that appears nowhere in the poem.

source.excerpt: Water, water, every where, / And all the boards did shrink; / Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink.
trail: The poem was “written…in 1797–98 and published in 1798” per Wikipedia.
The stanza on Project Gutenberg ends exactly “Nor any drop to drink.”
Wikipedia notes the lines are “usually given in a more natural modern phrasing” — i.e. commonly misquoted.
source.excerptNote: The becalmed mariner is surrounded by undrinkable sea. Note “every where” (two words) and “Nor any drop” — the exact wording the popular version rewrites.

sourceLink.text: Read the full poem at Project Gutenberg

source.rightsNote: “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” was first published in 1798 and revised in 1817 — both editions are long in the public domain. The popular “and not a drop to drink” wording, however, is a later paraphrase found in no edition of the poem.

author.heading: About Samuel Taylor Coleridge
author.bio: Samuel Taylor Coleridge was a founder of the English Romantic movement and, with William Wordsworth, co-author of Lyrical Ballads (1798). “The Rime of the Ancient Mariner” — his supernatural sea ballad of guilt, penance and the albatross — opened that volume and remains his most quoted work.

misattribution.heading: A misquote, not a misattribution
misattribution.intro: The right poet, the wrong words. Coleridge is correctly credited — but almost nobody quotes what he actually wrote.

items.why: The popular version replaces Coleridge’s “every where, / Nor any drop to drink” with the smoother “everywhere and not a drop to drink.” Wikipedia notes the lines are “usually given in a more natural modern phrasing” that departs from the original.
The line is often used to mean “plenty of something, none of it usable” — close to Coleridge’s intent, though he wrote of literal, undrinkable seawater around a becalmed ship.

misattribution.truthLine: Coleridge wrote “Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink” — confirmed in the poem’s text.

context.heading: Why the line endures
lead: In the poem, a sailor shoots an albatross and dooms his ship to a windless, cursed calm. The crew are trapped on a rotting deck ringed by an entire ocean they cannot drink — a perfect image of abundance that saves no one.
That paradox is why the line escaped the poem. It now stands for any glut that offers no relief: data without insight, choices without a good one, water everywhere and none to drink.
context.pull: Surrounded by an ocean, dying of thirst.
